title: Kafka vs Traditional Message Queues
description: Compare Kafka's log-based architecture with traditional message queues like RabbitMQ and Azure Service Bus.

data.text: Choosing between Kafka and a traditional message queue depends on your workload. Kafka excels at high-throughput, replayable event streams. Message queues like RabbitMQ and Azure Service Bus shine for task distribution, request routing, and guaranteed single-consumer delivery. Understanding their architectural differences helps you pick the right tool.

Kafka is built around a distributed, immutable log. Messages are persisted on disk and retained for a configurable period, allowing consumers to replay history. Traditional message queues typically delete messages after successful delivery, acting as transient buffers between producers and consumers.

cards.title: Apache Kafka
cards.description: A distributed event streaming platform optimized for high-throughput, durable logs and parallel consumption.
pros: Massive throughput (millions of messages per second)
Multiple consumer groups can read the same topic independently

cards.title: RabbitMQ / Azure Service Bus
cards.description: Traditional message brokers designed for reliable task delivery, request routing, and decoupled communication.
cons: Messages are typically deleted after delivery

data.title: Use Kafka when
items: You need to process millions of events per second.
Multiple downstream services must consume the same event stream.
You require long-term audit logs or event replay for analytics.
You are building event-driven microservices or CQRS pipelines.

data.title: Use a Message Queue when
items: You need simple work distribution across workers.
Request/reply or RPC-style communication is required.
Low latency and simple routing are more important than raw throughput.
Your team is already experienced with RabbitMQ or Azure Service Bus.

data.title: They Can Coexist
data.text: Kafka and message queues are not mutually exclusive. A common pattern is to use Kafka for high-volume event streams and a message queue for downstream task processing or notifications.

items.question: Can I use Kafka as a replacement for RabbitMQ?
items.answer: You can, but RabbitMQ remains simpler for basic task queues. Kafka's complexity pays off when you need replay, multiple consumers, or very high throughput.

items.question: Does Azure Service Bus support Kafka?
items.answer: Yes. Azure Event Hubs offers a Kafka-compatible endpoint, allowing Kafka clients to stream events into Azure without changing application code.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Kafka is a log-based stream processor; message queues are transient buffers.
Kafka enables multiple independent consumer groups; message queues typically target one consumer per message.
Choose Kafka for replay and scale; choose message queues for simplicity and routing.
data.takeaway: Match the broker to your consumption pattern, not the other way around.
